title: Hair & Cloth
subtitle: Follow through, bouncy hair, wind, flags, capes and landings

lessons.title: Hair Follows
lessons.summary: Hair drags behind, overshoots, then settles.

steps.title: Drag, overshoot, settle
steps.text: The ponytail is worked out like a chain on a spring.

beats.say: Hair is stuck on at the roots, but the rest is loose. So it never moves at exactly the same time as the head.
As the head speeds up, the ponytail drags behind. It's being pulled along by the root.
The head stops here. But the hair has its own speed now, so it keeps going.
It swings past the head, then back the other way, a little less each time.
Look closely. The bend travels down the hair from the root to the tip, one joint after another. Pros call that successive breaking of joints.
Then it hangs still. The tip is always the last part to stop.
So that's drag, overshoot, and settle. Hair, tails, ears, scarves, they all follow the same rule.

steps.title: Animate the follow through
steps.text: Six key frames: still, speeding up, stopping, swing past, swing back, rest. Draw the head and the ponytail on every frame.
steps.hint: Draw the head first, then the ponytail from the root to the tip. The tip moves the most.
tips: Still. The head on the left, the ponytail hanging straight down.
Speeding up. The head moves right and the hair drags out behind it.
The head stops. The hair is still trailing, it hasn't caught up yet.
Swing past. The hair flies forward, past the head.
Swing back. It comes back the other way, but not as far.
Rest. Hanging straight down again.

quiz.question: When a character stops suddenly, their ponytail...
quiz.explain: Loose things carry on moving: that's follow through.

quiz.question: Which part of the hair stops last?
quiz.explain: The root is fixed to the head; the tip is the loosest part.

lessons.title: Bouncy Hair
lessons.summary: Pigtails bob along, a beat behind the head.

steps.title: Pigtails on a bounce
steps.text: The head bobs up and down, like when someone walks. The pigtails follow late.

beats.say: Here's a head bobbing up and down, like it's walking. Watch the pigtails.
When the head goes up, the pigtails get left behind for a moment. They're heavy, so they lag.
When the head comes down, the pigtails are still on their way up, then they flop down late.
Follow the tip. It moves more than the root, and a little after it.
This little delay is overlap. It turns a stiff head into one that feels soft and bouncy.

steps.title: Animate bouncy pigtails
steps.text: Eight frames that loop. Draw the head and both pigtails on every frame.
steps.hint: Draw the head first. The pigtail tips are always a step behind the head.
tips: The middle of the bob. Head and pigtails at rest.
The head rises. The pigtails start to get left behind.
The head at its highest. The tips are still low, lagging behind.
The head starts down. Now the tips are swinging up.
Back to the middle. The tips are at their highest.
The head drops. The tips are still up, about to flop.
The head at its lowest. The tips are on their way down.
Coming back up. Then it loops to frame 1.

quiz.question: The head goes up. Where are the pigtail tips?
quiz.explain: Loose parts follow a little later.

lessons.title: Hair in the Wind
lessons.summary: Waves roll down the hair from the root to the tip.

steps.title: Wind in the hair
steps.text: Three locks of hair blowing back. Each one is a wave travelling from the head to the tip.

beats.say: Wind is blowing from the right, so the hair streams out to the left.
Look at one lock. The wave starts at the head and rolls all the way out to the tip.
The roots hardly move. The tips flick the most. That's what makes it feel light.
And each lock is a little out of step with the others. If they all wave together, it looks like one stiff sheet.
The last frame flows straight back into the first, so the wind can blow forever.

steps.title: Animate hair in the wind
steps.text: Six frames that loop. Draw the head and the three locks of hair on every frame.
steps.hint: Keep the roots still. Move the wave a little further toward the tip on each frame.
tips: The head and three locks blowing back. Notice where each wave is.
Move every wave a little further out toward the tips.
Further again. The bumps keep rolling out.
The tips flick as the waves reach them.
New waves start back near the head.
Nearly back where you started. It loops to frame 1.

quiz.question: In the wind, which way do the waves travel along the hair?
choices: From the root to the tip
From the tip to the root
quiz.explain: The head holds the root, so the waves start there and roll out.

quiz.question: Should every lock of hair wave exactly together?
choices: No, a little out of step looks natural
Yes, all at the same time
quiz.explain: Offsetting them stops it looking like one stiff sheet.

steps.title: How a flag waves
steps.text: The pole holds one edge still. Waves run out to the free end.

beats.say: A flag is cloth held still along one edge, at the pole. Everything else is free.
The wind sends waves along it, from the pole out to the free end. Watch a bump travel.
Near the pole the cloth barely moves. The free corner flaps the most.
The top and bottom edges wave together, so the whole flag ripples like one piece of cloth.

steps.title: Animate a waving flag
steps.text: Six frames that loop. Draw the flag on every frame. The pole is already there.
steps.hint: The edge at the pole never moves. Move each wave a little further out each frame.
tips: The flag with its waves. The pole edge stays straight.
Shift every wave a little away from the pole.
A little further again.
The free corner flips as a wave reaches it.
A new wave starts by the pole.
Almost back to frame 1, so it loops smoothly.

quiz.question: Which way do the waves travel on a flag?
choices: From the pole to the free end
From the free end to the pole
quiz.explain: The pole holds one end, so the waves start there and run outward.

lessons.title: Capes & Scarves
lessons.summary: Cloth that drags and ripples behind a runner.

steps.title: A cape on a run
steps.text: A runner with a cape. The cape is attached at the shoulders.

beats.say: A cape is like hair and a flag mixed together. It's pinned at the shoulders and free at the end.
The runner pushes through the air, so the cape flies out flat behind them.
Waves ripple from the shoulders to the tip, just like on a flag.
The faster the run, the flatter it flies. Slow down, and it droops and swings more.
It also bobs with the body, a little behind. Every step jiggles the cloth.

steps.title: Animate the cape
steps.text: Four frames that loop. The runner is a faint guide; draw just the cape on every frame.
steps.hint: Start every cape at the shoulders. Move the ripple toward the tip each frame.
tips: Start at the shoulders and sweep the cape out behind, with a ripple in it.
The ripple moves further toward the tip.
Further again, and the tip flicks.
A new ripple starts by the shoulders. It loops to frame 1.

quiz.question: What makes a cape fly flatter behind a character?
quiz.explain: More speed means more wind pushing the cape back.

lessons.title: Cloth That Lands
lessons.summary: Cloth floats as it falls, then drops, bounces and settles.

steps.title: A skirt on landing
steps.text: A bean in a skirt drops to the floor. Only the skirt is worked out as loose cloth.

beats.say: Watch the skirt as this little bean drops down and lands.
While it falls, air pushes up under the cloth, so the skirt floats up and flares out.
The body lands, but the skirt is still floating. It hasn't got the message yet.
Then it drops, right past where it normally hangs. It goes too far down.
It springs back up a little, then down again, a bit less each time, until it rests.
Hair, capes, skirts and ears all do this. Up on the fall, past the rest on the landing, then settle.

steps.title: Animate the skirt
steps.text: Eight frames, holds already set. The bean is a faint guide; draw just the skirt on every frame.
steps.hint: Falling, the hem floats up and flares. After landing it drops too low, bounces, then settles.
tips: Falling. The hem is lifted a little by the air.
Falling faster. The skirt floats up higher and flares out.
Almost down. The skirt is at its floatiest.
The landing. The body squashes, but the skirt is still up.
The skirt drops past its rest. Make it hang a bit too low and narrow.
It springs back up a little.
A smaller dip down again.
Settled. The skirt hangs at its normal shape.

quiz.question: While a character falls, a loose skirt...
quiz.explain: Air pushes up under the cloth as it falls.

quiz.question: Just after landing, the cloth...
choices: Drops past its rest, then bounces and settles
Stops the moment the feet touch
quiz.explain: Cloth keeps moving after the body stops: follow through.
